title: Hello, my name is Ana
goal: Greet anyone safely, give your name, ask for the other person's, and say your first correct Greek sentence — one that **must** contain the verb "to be".
bekal: greet people formally and casually, and know the difference
say your name and ask other people theirs
say thank you, sorry, and excuse me
build "I am X" sentences with the verb είμαι
negate with δεν and answer with όχι

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — First day of the course
dialogs.intro: Ana, a student from Indonesia, walks into a Greek class in Athens and sits down next to someone she doesn't know yet. Notice that almost every sentence below uses a word meaning "am / is / are" — and that this word can never be dropped.

lines.speaker: Γιάννης:
lines.id: My name is Yannis. And you?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. My name is Ana. I'm from Indonesia.
lines.literal: I-rejoice — much. me — they-call — Anna. I-am — from — the — Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Γιάννης:
lines.id: Ah, Indonesia! Are you a student?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you?

lines.speaker: Γιάννης:
lines.id: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.
lines.literal: I — not — I-am — student. I-am — teacher.

lines.speaker: Γιάννης:
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a good day, Ana!
lines.literal: please / you're-welcome. good — to-you — day, Anna!

notes: **Greek needs its verb "to be", just like English.** *Είμαι φοιτήτρια* = "I am a student". ⚠️ *Εγώ φοιτήτρια* ("me student") is **wrong** and sounds like a telegram. In the present tense, είμαι can never go missing.

**What you *can* drop is the pronoun.** *Είμαι* already means "I am" — the ending **-μαι** tells you who. Use Εγώ only for emphasis or contrast, exactly as Γιάννης does: *Εγώ δεν είμαι φοιτητής* — "*I'm* not a student, though". Saying εγώ every time sounds as heavy as "I myself" would in English.

**Γεια σου is casual, Γεια σας is formal.** Γεια literally means "health", so a Greek greeting really says "health to you". Γεια σου is for friends and people your age; Γεια σας is for strangers, older people, officials — and for more than one person at once. ⚠️ This one word covers "hello" **and** "goodbye", just like *ciao*.

**Με λένε literally means "they call me".** Not "my name is". Who "they" are is never explained — just take it as one chunk: *Με λένε ___*. ⚠️ And your name goes in the **object** form, so Γιάννη**ς** becomes Γιάννη. Luckily, names that don't end in -ος/-ης don't change at all: *Με λένε Άννα, Με λένε Μπούντι.*

**Καλημέρα until about noon, Καλησπέρα after that, Καληνύχτα only when parting for the night.** ⚠️ Καληνύχτα is "good night", never "good evening" — saying it as you arrive at a party sounds as if you're already leaving.

**Συγγνώμη and Λυπάμαι don't weigh the same.** Συγγνώμη (*see-GHNOH-mee*) is for small things: interrupting, squeezing past, a wrong guess. Λυπάμαι (*lee-PAH-meh*), literally "I am sad", is for things that are truly sad — condolences, or turning down a big request. Saying Λυπάμαι after guessing someone's job wrong sounds overdone.
**Παρακαλώ: one word, three jobs.** It means "please", "here you go", and "you're welcome", and you'll use it dozens of times a day. On the phone it even means "hello?". Literally: "I beg".
⚠️ **Look at the question mark in this dialogue: ; not ?.** Εσείς**;** means "And you?" — it's not a sentence trailing off. It will look odd until about Unit 5, and then never again.

grammars.title: Είμαι — the one verb to learn by heart today
body: This is the first and most frequently used verb in Greek. It's irregular, so there's no pattern to guess — learn all six lines at once, out loud, until they come out without thinking.
after: ⚠️ **είναι covers two lines at once**: "he/she is" and "they are". Only the context and the noun tell them apart. Good news — one less form to learn.

To negate, put **δεν** (*dhehn*) right before the verb: *Δεν είμαι φοιτητής* — I'm not a student. ⚠️ **δεν** negates a verb, while **όχι** (*OH-khee*) is the stand-alone answer "no". Don't mix them up: the question *Είσαι φοιτητής;* is answered *Όχι, δεν είμαι.*

grammars.title: Εσύ and εσείς — two levels of politeness
body: Greek separates a friendly "you" from a polite "you", like French *tu* and *vous*. English lost this distinction centuries ago, but in Greek the choice is **compulsory** and you hear it straight away in the verb ending.

head: ΕΣΥ (casual)
ΕΣΕΙΣ (polite)
rows: friends, people your age, family, children
strangers, older people, bosses, officials — and more than one person

after: ⚠️ A rule of thumb for newcomers: **use εσείς until the Greek person switches to εσύ**. The switch usually happens quietly, without announcement — as soon as the other person uses εσύ, follow suit. Using εσείς with someone your age sounds a little stiff; using εσύ with an older person or an official sounds rude. Of the two mistakes, the first is far cheaper.
Greeks switch to εσύ much faster than the French or Germans. Among people the same age, εσύ is often used from the first minute. With someone clearly older, εσείς lasts a long time.

sections.title: Phrases to keep in your pocket on day one

blocks.text: These twelve phrases cover nearly all first-day small talk. Learn them whole, as chunks; the grammar will untangle itself in the coming units.

head: ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΑ
Say it
English
rows: Please / Here you go / You're welcome
How do you say it in Greek?

blocks.text: The two sentences near the end aren't just vocabulary — they're learning tools. Once you can ask "what is this" and "how do you say it in Greek", every Greek around you becomes a walking dictionary. And **εντάξει** will be the word you say most often for as long as you live in Greece.

blocks.title: Τι κάνεις; and its little trap
items: **Τι κάνεις;** (*tee KAH-nees*) literally means "what are you doing?" and is used for "how are you?". The polite form is **Τι κάνετε;** (*tee KAH-neh-teh*).
Standard answers: **Καλά** (fine), **Μια χαρά** (great, literally "one joy"), **Έτσι κι έτσι** (so-so, literally "like this and like this"), **Χάλια** (awful).
The polite reply adds **Εσύ;** or **Εσείς;** — "and you?". Leaving the question unreturned sounds cold.
⚠️ Unlike English *How are you?*, Τι κάνεις; is **not** empty small talk tossed at a cashier. You ask it of people you know, and the answer is actually listened to — sometimes for five minutes.

vocab.en: please, here you go, you're welcome

exercises.prompt: Translate into Greek. Remember: the verb "to be" must never go missing.
Fill in the blanks with the right form of είμαι (είμαι, είσαι, είναι, είμαστε, είστε).
Put the words in the right order.
Choose the right phrase. Write your answer in Greek letters.
items: You walk into the staff room at eight in the morning. You say ____.
You didn't catch what someone said. You say ____.
You step on someone's foot on the metro. You say ____.
Someone has just helped you. You say ____.
You're leaving the office and saying goodbye to your boss. You say ____.

answers: Γεια σας! — Με λένε Άννα. — Είμαι φοιτήτρια. — Δεν είναι δάσκαλος. — Πώς σας λένε; — Είμαι από την Ινδονησία.
Με λένε Άννα. — Δεν είμαι φοιτητής. — Χαίρω πολύ. — Όλα καλά. — Πώς σας λένε;
Καλημέρα — Δεν καταλαβαίνω — Συγγνώμη — Ευχαριστώ — Γεια σας
